title: Trust Doesn't Travel Over Zoom
author: Joel Trammell
summary: Joel Trammell uses the election-season rally as an analogy to argue that CEOs have misread video as simply the more efficient way to communicate. A rally is not an informational event, he says; people attend to see the candidate and decide whether to believe him, and the same is true when a CEO must persuade an organization to change. He offers five principles: communication is the CEO's ultimate skill and works best in person, trust is hard to build over a screen, the office is more than a place to work, a CEO who wants people in the office must show up first, and the screen should be used to inform while presence is used to persuade. He draws on Wharton research by Cappelli and Nehmeh and on the older practice of management by walking around, and he notes the risk that office advocacy sounds like distrust. Routine reviews can run on Zoom, but major strategic shifts, reorganizations and asks for sacrifice belong in the room, followed by the unscripted conversations afterward.
points: Video is efficient for exchanging information but weak at changing minds, because the CEO cannot read confusion or objection when cameras are off and faces are thumbnails.
Management by walking around deserves a revival, and the argument strengthens in the AI era when polished memos and personalised messages are cheap but personal credibility is not.
Return-to-office policies fail when leaders exempt themselves, so a CEO mandating office days while working from a distant home has undermined the policy before it starts.
Employers and employees see remote work differently, so a CEO who wants more time together has to explain why rather than appear to monitor people.
A practical rule: use the screen for status updates and routine decisions, and be in the room for strategy shifts, reorganizations and anything that asks people to sacrifice.
quotes: Politicians understand something many executives forgot during the remote-work years: a rally is not an informational event. Nobody leaves the event knowing more policy than they could have read on the website.

Many have drawn the wrong conclusion from the ease and ubiquity of video, thinking of it as more efficient. It is not, and it is also very bad at the one thing a CEO most needs to do: persuade people to change.
On Zoom, half the cameras may be off and the rest of the audience is reduced to thumbnails. The people with the strongest objections may be the least likely to speak up.

I’ve written before about Leadership by ESP, the CEO who assumes the organization knows what he is thinking because it is so clear in his own head. Remote communication makes that failure even easier. A CEO who can’t see the audience can’t see the confusion either.
A CEO who flies to a branch office to discuss a difficult change is communicating something before saying a word: these employees and their concerns are important enough to warrant the trip.

A CEO who mandates three office days a week while working remotely from a home two states away has undermined the policy before it begins. The same is true when members of the executive team enjoy special arrangements unavailable to the rest of the organization.
The distinction I would make is between communication intended primarily to exchange information and communication intended to change people’s minds or behavior.
Politicians keep holding rallies because, election after election, they find that people are more likely to follow someone they have met and decided to trust. Employees are no different.
